questions.question: What are the three pillars of observability?
questions.explanation: The three pillars: Logs (discrete events), Metrics (numeric measurements over time), Traces (request flow across services). Together they provide comprehensive system visibility for debugging and monitoring.

questions.question: What is the purpose of observability?

options.text: To understand system behavior and diagnose issues from external outputs

questions.explanation: Observability enables understanding internal system state from external outputs (logs, metrics, traces). Essential for debugging production issues, understanding behavior, and answering questions you didn't anticipate.

questions.question: What are logs?

options.text: Discrete, timestamped records of events that occurred in the system

questions.explanation: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events: errors, state changes, user actions. Rich context (stack traces, request details). Good for debugging specific issues. Challenge: high volume, searching at scale.

questions.question: What are metrics?

options.text: Numeric measurements aggregated over time (counters, gauges, histograms)

questions.explanation: Metrics are numeric values tracked over time: request count, latency percentiles, CPU usage, error rate. Aggregated and efficient to store. Good for dashboards, alerting, trend analysis. Less detail than logs.

questions.question: What are distributed traces?

options.text: Records of request flow across multiple services, showing timing and dependencies

questions.explanation: Traces track requests across service boundaries: which services were called, in what order, how long each took. Essential for debugging latency issues and understanding request flow in microservices.

questions.question: When should you use logs vs metrics vs traces? (Choose the best matches)

options.text: Traces for understanding request flow across services

questions.explanation: Use all three: Logs for detailed debugging (what exactly happened), Metrics for monitoring and alerting (is the system healthy?), Traces for understanding distributed request flow (where is latency?). Complementary tools.

questions.question: What is a 'span' in distributed tracing?

options.text: A unit of work within a trace, representing an operation in one service

questions.explanation: Span represents a single operation: service call, database query, etc. Contains: operation name, start/end time, tags, logs. Spans are linked to form traces. Parent-child relationships show call hierarchy.

questions.question: What is cardinality in metrics and why does it matter?

options.text: Number of unique label combinations; high cardinality increases storage and query costs

questions.explanation: Cardinality = unique label combinations. High cardinality (e.g., user_id as label) explodes storage and slows queries. Use low-cardinality labels (status_code, endpoint). Aggregate high-cardinality data differently.

questions.question: True or False: Observability and monitoring are the same thing.
questions.explanation: Monitoring: watching known metrics, alerting on predefined conditions. Observability: ability to understand ANY system state from outputs, including unknown-unknowns. Observability enables exploring questions you didn't anticipate.

questions.question: What is a correlation ID?

options.text: A unique identifier passed through all services handling a request, linking logs and traces

questions.explanation: Correlation ID (trace ID, request ID) is passed through all services handling a request. Enables linking logs, traces, and metrics for a single request across the distributed system. Essential for debugging.

questions.question: Which tools are commonly used for each observability pillar? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Logs: ELK Stack, Splunk, CloudWatch Logs

questions.explanation: Common tools: Logs (ELK/Elasticsearch, Splunk, CloudWatch), Metrics (Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog), Traces (Jaeger, Zipkin, X-Ray). Many platforms now offer unified observability across all three pillars.

questions.question: What is the challenge of observability in microservices?

options.text: Requests span multiple services; correlating data across services is complex

questions.explanation: Microservices challenge: a single request touches many services. Logs are scattered, metrics are per-service, failures can occur anywhere. Need distributed tracing and correlation IDs to connect the dots.
